stem: A payments risk lead must approve how the fraud-review threshold is tuned before checkout rollout. A false rejection blocks a legitimate customer's payment; a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next business day. Which threshold policy should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Return to discovery to re-price both error directions before making any threshold decision.
Optimize the model for the highest overall accuracy across both error types on the evaluation set.
Bias the threshold toward recall and route flagged cases to human review before blocking any payment.
Bias the threshold toward precision, accepting more missed fraud cases to avoid blocking legitimate payments.

whyRight: The false rejection is irreversible at the moment of checkout, while a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next day; the threshold should minimize the costlier, unrecoverable error rather than treat both directions as equally acceptable.

whyWrong.A: The stem already prices both directions — irreversible versus next-day recoverable — so returning to discovery discards evidence already given instead of acting on it.
whyWrong.B: A flat accuracy target weights both error directions equally, but the stem states one direction is irreversible and the other recoverable.
whyWrong.C: This directly increases the false-rejection rate, which the stem already establishes as the irreversible, costlier error — the opposite of what the stated asymmetry requires.

t1Clause: a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next business day
lessonKey: action bias higher precision set threshold toward

stem: A CFO is deciding whether to renew a document-processing contract and needs a defensible number before the board meeting. The architect currently declines to quote any accuracy figure, citing wide variance across document types. What should the architect do instead?

opts.t: Report figures segmented by document type, the measurement method, and the end-to-end outcome including human review.
Report a single blended accuracy figure, since it is honest given the stated method and evaluation set.
Report only the underlying model's classification accuracy, since that is the metric the CFO originally asked about.
Decline to provide any figure until the sponsor accepts that accuracy depends on document type.

whyRight: The CFO has a budget decision to make and cannot make it on a qualitative answer; segmented figures with the measurement basis and end-to-end outcome, including the human-review step, give a defensible number to plan against.

whyWrong.B: The stem states performance varies sharply by document type, so a single blended figure is contradicted by the evidence already given, not merely imprecise.
whyWrong.C: This states a real figure but omits the human-review step and the end-to-end outcome, which is what the CFO's budget decision actually depends on.
whyWrong.D: The CFO's renewal decision needs a number to plan against; declining to quantify is not acceptable even though the underlying variability claim is true.

t1Clause: citing wide variance across document types

stem: After a polished pre-launch demo, a sponsor now assumes the system performs at that level for all incoming volume and is building next quarter's staffing plan on that assumption. What should the architect put in place before rollout?

opts.t: Establish a recurring review that reports real performance on real production inputs against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Send a detailed written memo to the sponsor explaining the system's real performance and current limitations.
Restructure users' ad hoc feedback into a structured log of input, output, expected output, and reviewer feeding the evaluation set.
Have the sponsor formally accept the demo's results as the system's expected production baseline going forward.

whyRight: Expectations re-inflate after every demonstration, so a one-time correction cannot hold against continuous drift; only a recurring measurement against agreed criteria keeps the sponsor's plan anchored to real production performance rather than a single favorable demo.

whyWrong.B: A memo corrects today's understanding but expectations re-inflate at the next demonstration; the table treats a one-time correction as necessary, not sufficient, against continuous drift.
whyWrong.C: This is the right fix for scattered chat-channel complaints, but the stem describes overconfidence from a clean demo, not ungathered failure reports.
whyWrong.D: This locks in a single favorable measurement as a standing commitment instead of establishing the recurring review that continuous expectation drift actually requires.

lessonKey: against agreed criteria establish inputs performance real recurring review showing

stem: A model-tier decision was recorded a year ago under a strict latency ceiling that has since been relaxed by the platform team. The evaluation numbers and the rejected alternatives from that decision are unchanged. What should the architect check first?

opts.t: Schedule a walkthrough session where the original architects explain their reasoning to the questioning team.
Re-run the original latency and quality benchmark from scratch on the current infrastructure.
Move immediately to a higher-capability model, since the ceiling that constrained the original choice no longer applies.
Retrieve the decision record's stated constraint and re-evaluate the original trade-off now that the ceiling has moved.

whyRight: The record exists for exactly this moment: when a driving constraint changes, checking what was recorded against the new condition is the fastest way to tell whether the original decision still holds, before any component is re-built.

whyWrong.A: A walkthrough transfers the reasoning once to whoever attends, but it goes stale immediately and gives the team nothing durable to check the next time a constraint moves.
whyWrong.B: This discards a year of recorded evaluation numbers and rebuilds them before checking whether the ceiling change even affects the original trade-off.
whyWrong.C: This spends money on a capability upgrade before confirming, against the recorded trade-off, whether the relaxed ceiling actually changes which tier is warranted.

t1Clause: The evaluation numbers and the rejected alternatives from that decision are unchanged
lessonKey: against check constraint evaluate re recorded

stem: A successful pilot served 60 users: a 1-in-500 failure occurred twice across 200 cases, and human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume. Before recommending rollout to 1,200 users, select two points the architect's report to sponsor leadership must include.

opts.t: Rate limits and infrastructure capacity for 1,200-user volume are necessary and should headline the report as the binding constraint.
The report should recommend a higher-capability model ahead of rollout to preempt the wider input variety at scale.
The 1-in-500 failure rate should be planned for as a routine, several-times-daily event at full volume.
The 12% human-review load should be converted into a staffing line sized for 1,200-user volume.

whyRight: Both are pilot-to-scale assumptions that break at higher volume: a rare failure becomes routine at scale, and human review invisible in the pilot must become an explicit staffing line before the budget is approved by leadership.

whyWrong.A: Capacity planning is necessary but the table explicitly treats it as the visible constraint, not the binding one — the input-distribution risk is what actually determines whether rollout succeeds.
whyWrong.B: This spends on a bigger model before anyone has characterised the inputs at 800-user volume, skipping the assumption audit the report is meant to deliver.

t1Clause: human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume

stem: A compliance team asks an architect to commit a fraud-triage model to "95% accuracy" before the next audit, without stating whether a missed case or a false alarm costs more. What should happen before a threshold is set?

opts.t: Return to discovery and price both error directions before setting any threshold.
Bias the model toward recall and route every flagged case to human review.
Commit to the 95% target, since both error directions are likely low-cost and easily corrected.
Benchmark several candidate models against the 95% figure to find the one that reaches it most reliably.

whyRight: The sponsor has stated a number but not which error direction costs more; a flat accuracy target cannot encode that asymmetry, so pricing both directions and letting the ratio set the threshold and review placement comes before any commitment is made.

whyWrong.B: Biasing toward recall is correct once the asymmetry is known and priced; here neither direction's cost has been established, so the direction chosen is a guess.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the costs are unstated, not that they are low; assuming both directions are cheap contradicts what the compliance team actually said.
whyWrong.D: A benchmark produces a number before there is a target error cost to interpret it against, the same gap a bare accuracy figure already has.

t1Clause: without stating whether a missed case or a false alarm costs more

stem: A product lead confirms the disputed-claims segment carries no regulator attestation requirement, yet a fifth of cases still route to a reviewer even as model accuracy keeps improving. What should the architect tell them?

opts.t: Explain that AI systems are probabilistic and human review remains a safety best practice for this segment.
Say the system cannot verify its own output against ground truth, and that better evaluation data could close it.
Commit to removing the reviewer once accuracy on this segment crosses a stated threshold.
Refuse to remove the reviewer, citing the segment's regulatory attestation requirement, and quantify what the segment is worth.

whyRight: The segment's limit is that the system cannot verify its own output against ground truth, not a missing attestation; naming that distinction points to the actual remedy, richer evaluation data, instead of a generic caution or a false regulatory citation.

whyWrong.A: This is true of AI systems generally but names nothing specific; the stakeholder still cannot tell whether this segment is closable or a standing limit.
whyWrong.C: Accuracy improving is not the same as having verified ground truth; committing to a threshold promises a guarantee the missing evaluation data does not yet support.
whyWrong.D: The stem states no regulator attestation applies to this segment; citing one as the reason for keeping the reviewer contradicts the fact already given.

lessonKey: against cannot cases check ground output own say so system these truth

stem: A support team has logged the input, the output, and a reviewer's note for every user-reported failure in a shared tracker for six months, but the pre-release evaluation set has not grown since launch. What does this represent?

opts.t: A working feedback loop, since every case already carries an input, an output, and a reviewer's note.
Restructure this as a loop that captures input, output, expected output, and reviewer, then feeds the evaluation set.
Sufficient, because a named product owner already reviews the tracker weekly and can act on trends.
A broken loop: the system stays measured against an evaluation set that diverges further from production inputs every week.

whyRight: The tracker already captures each case's input, output, and reviewer note, so the defect is not structural; the loop is broken because none of that captured detail is feeding the evaluation set, which keeps aging against a population the system no longer sees.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the evaluation set has not grown since launch; calling the arrangement working directly contradicts that stated fact.
whyWrong.B: That rebuild is the fix when nothing is being captured yet; here input, output, and reviewer notes already exist, and the missing link is the feed to the evaluation set.
whyWrong.C: A weekly review of the tracker is not the same mechanism as growing the evaluation set; the two remain disconnected regardless of how often anyone reads the tracker.

t1Clause: has logged the input, the output, and a reviewer's note for every user-reported failure in a shared tracker

stem: Nine months after a document-extraction pipeline shipped, a team weighs replacing the model with a larger-context version; the only record is a component diagram and inventory, and the latency budget is unchanged. What should they check first?

opts.t: Check whether the alternatives, trade-offs, and constraint behind the model choice were ever recorded at all.
Check the recorded latency ceiling that drove the original choice, and re-evaluate the decision against it.
Commission a more detailed component diagram and an updated service inventory before deciding.
Ship the larger-context model now, and audit a sample of outputs after the change to confirm nothing broke.

whyRight: A diagram and an inventory show what the system is, not why the model tier was chosen; before swapping it, the team needs to know whether the alternatives, trade-offs, and constraint behind that choice were ever written down.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the record shows a latency ceiling was ever captured; there is no recorded constraint for this option to check against.
whyWrong.C: More detail in the diagram and inventory still describes what the system is; it does not supply the missing reasoning behind the original choice.
whyWrong.D: Shipping first and auditing outputs afterward risks a regression the missing rationale might have flagged in advance, on a change already worth pausing to check.

t1Clause: the only record is a component diagram and inventory
